title: My Orders shows "No orders found" when the orders API is failing — /api/customer-orders 502s on the compose stack

body:
**Found while running the browser falsification #457 asked for.** It is a *different* defect from
#457 and a more severe one, so it is filed separately rather than folded in.

## The customer session ends after 300 seconds, whatever the customer is doing

Measured 2026-08-02 against the live Compose stack on `main`, with a customer registered through the
real PKCE flow (Keycloak `jtoye-customers` / `storefront-client`, S256).

**Two arms, both ending logged out:**

| arm | what the customer did | result |
|---|---|---|
| idle | signed in, sat on `/` for ~5 min, returned to `/shop` | marker **cleared to `null`**, nav shows `Sign in` |
| **active** | signed in, navigated `/shop` and `/shop/orders` continuously for ~6 min | expiry stayed pinned at its original value through **4 minutes of navigation**; logged out at exactly **300s** |

The active arm is the one that matters. The customer was continuously using the very surfaces that
*do* consult the session, and was signed out on schedule anyway. **Activity does not extend the
session.**

## Mechanism — confirmed in code, not inferred from the symptom

- `frontend/app/api/customer-auth/session/route.ts` decides `authenticated` **solely** on the
  ID-token cookie's `claims.exp < now`. There is no renewal branch.
- The refresh token **is** issued and stored, HttpOnly, `maxAge = 60 * 60 * 24 * 30` (**30 days**) —
  `frontend/app/api/customer-auth/login/route.ts:65`.
- **Nothing ever redeems it.** `grant_type: "refresh_token"` appears exactly once in the frontend, in
  `frontend/auth.ts` — the **operator** NextAuth path on the `jtoye-dev` realm. The customer path has
  no equivalent.

Realm `jtoye-customers`, read from the live admin API:

| setting | value |
|---|---|
| `accessTokenLifespan` | **300s** |
| `ssoSessionIdleTimeout` | 1800s (30 min) |
| `ssoSessionMaxLifespan` | 7200s (2 h) |
| `revokeRefreshToken` | `true` |
| `refreshTokenMaxReuse` | `0` |

**The IdP session outlives the app session**, which is the clearest statement of the bug: after the
idle arm logged the customer out, clicking `Sign in` returned them to `/shop` signed in **with no
credential prompt** — Keycloak's SSO session was alive the whole time. The app threw away a session
the IdP was still happy to honour, while holding an unused 30-day refresh token.

## Impact

This is a food-ordering storefront. A customer browsing a menu, reading allergen information and
building a basket is logged out mid-order after five minutes. It is also the likelier mechanism
behind the owner-reported *"going home when logged in logs one out"* (#457) — #457's header
blindness explains the *appearance* on `/` and `/track`; this explains an actual logout on any
surface.

## Fix direction

Redeem the refresh token server-side when the access token is near or past expiry, and re-issue the
cookies. Two constraints for whoever implements:

1. **Rotation is enforced** — `revokeRefreshToken=true` with `refreshTokenMaxReuse=0`, so the
   *rotated* refresh token from each response must be persisted. Reusing the old one will be
   rejected and will log the customer out exactly as today.
2. Keep the refresh strictly server-side. The current design deliberately keeps tokens in HttpOnly
   cookies so they never reach JS (`customer-auth.ts:286`) — that property must survive the fix.

Bound the session by the IdP's own SSO settings rather than by the access-token lifespan, so
`ssoSessionIdleTimeout` / `ssoSessionMaxLifespan` become the real limits.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] A customer who signs in and keeps using the storefront is still signed in after **10 minutes**
      — more than two access-token lifespans. Verified in a browser across the boundary, not by unit
      test, since the current code passes every unit test while failing this.
- [ ] A customer idle on `/` past 300s and returning to `/shop` is still signed in.
- [ ] The rotated refresh token is persisted — proven by surviving **two** consecutive refreshes, not
      one. A single-refresh test passes even when rotation is mishandled.
- [ ] The access/refresh/id tokens still never appear in `document.cookie` or any JS-readable
      storage. Asserted in the browser.
- [ ] Sign-out still terminates the session at Keycloak, not just locally.
- [ ] The logged-out path is unchanged for genuinely anonymous visitors: `/api/customer-auth/session`
      still answers `200 { authenticated: false }`, never 401 (backlog #13).

## Evidence

Full two-arm capture, timestamps, realm settings and the code trace are in the session evidence
write-up; the arms are reproducible with the steps above in ~12 minutes.

Related: #457 (the cosmetic half — a session-blind public header), #461 (payments).

title: Customer session ends after 300s regardless of activity — the 30-day refresh token is stored and never redeemed

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (item 5). **Parked pending measurement, then measured** — this issue exists because the measurement came back actionable and contradicted the obvious explanation.

## Reported

> *"'My orders' takes too long rolling the disk. That page can load much faster I strongly believe. I believe the same applies to all pages. They should all be fast and responsive."*

## Measured — the backend is not the cause

Against the running stack:

| target | result |
|---|---|
| vendor orders API, warm | **13–17 ms** |
| vendor orders API, first (cold) | 293 ms |
| `/shop` (server-rendered page) | **12 ms** |

So the API is not slow, and a server-rendered page on this stack is effectively instant. The spinner is **client-side**, and "make the query faster" would have been wasted work.

## The actual cause

`frontend/app/shop/orders/page.tsx` is `"use client"` (line 1) — the whole page is a client component. The sequence a customer waits through is therefore:

1. download the JS bundle
2. hydrate
3. `useEffect` fires → `fetchOrders()` (`:206-208`)
4. `fetch("/api/customer-orders?size=100")` (`:187`)
5. only now does `loading` clear (`:159`, `:237`)

**Nothing renders from the server at all.** The spinner covers bundle + hydration + a request that itself takes ~15 ms. That is a rendering-strategy problem, not a data problem.

Two related observations from the same file, not separate issues but worth fixing together:

- **`?size=100` fetches up to 100 orders to render a list.** There is no pagination in the view. Note this also sits exactly on the documented silent page cap (a `?size` above 100 is capped with no signal), so the page is coupled to a limit it never states.
- **A 15 s polling interval** (`:214`) re-runs the same fetch indefinitely while the page is open.

## Why the owner's wider point is the important half

> *"I believe the same applies to all pages."*

Worth taking seriously as a **systemic** question rather than one page. The measurement above shows the two rendering strategies produce wildly different perceived performance on identical infrastructure — 12 ms server-rendered versus bundle-plus-hydrate-plus-fetch. Any other `"use client"` page fetching its own data on mount has the same shape.

Related but distinct, already tracked: CLS breaching the repo's own budget on three routes. That is layout stability; this is time-to-content. Both are web-performance, and both should be measured at the same throttled mobile profile.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] The orders list renders meaningful content **without waiting for a client-side fetch** — server-rendered, streamed, or otherwise not gated behind hydration.
- [ ] Measured at the repo's declared **throttled mobile profile** (390 px, 4× CPU, Fast 3G), not on unthrottled localhost — a localhost measurement will look fine and prove nothing, which is the documented trap and is precisely why the backend looked innocent until it was measured properly.
- [ ] The pre-fix number is captured first, so the improvement is falsifiable rather than asserted.
- [ ] An **inventory** of other `"use client"` pages that fetch on mount, so the systemic half of the report is answered rather than one page fixed. Silent truncation of that list is a finding in itself — say what was not covered.
- [ ] The polling interval and the unpaginated `size=100` fetch are addressed or deliberately justified in writing.
- [ ] No route regresses on CLS while improving time-to-content — the two are easy to trade off against each other by accident.
title: UX-7: My Orders spinner is client-side rendering, not a slow API — measured 13-17ms API vs a fully "use client" page (item 5)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (item 11). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"If a user is using username/password and not social signup/login, then I think there should be a 2-factor authentication that confirms the number they are using is valid/acceptable, or the social medium they are engaging on can be trusted."*

## Verified

- `CONFIGURE_TOTP` in the **staff** realm is `enabled=true, defaultAction=false` — the required action is *available*, but no user is ever asked to configure it. This is Keycloak's stock default, not a decision that was made.
- The **customer** realm template (`realm-export-customers.template.json`) has **no `requiredActions` block at all**.
- **No phone verification exists anywhere** — `verifyPhone` returns 0 hits across the frontend, core and Keycloak configuration.

So a password-only customer account today is confirmed by nothing. No second factor, no phone check, and no verified contact channel.

## Why this matters here specifically, beyond generic account security

The owner's framing is the useful one: this is less about account takeover and more about **whether the contact channel can be trusted** — and that is load-bearing for two other things in flight:

- **The payment-link model** (companion issue) sends a bearer payment credential to *"the telephone number they've called on"*. If that number was never verified, the link can be delivered to an unverified destination.
- **Order notifications** already carry customer detail by email through the Phase 22 lifecycle.

A social login carries an identity assertion from a provider that already did this work. A username/password signup carries none. That asymmetry is exactly what the owner identified.

## Design questions to settle first

1. **What is being verified — possession of a phone number, or a second factor at login?** They are different features. Phone verification at signup answers "can we trust this channel"; TOTP/SMS at login answers "is this the account holder". The owner's framing points at the **first** as the priority.
2. **Which flows require it?** Payment-link delivery is the strongest candidate; requiring it at signup adds friction at the worst moment in the funnel.
3. **Is social login treated as pre-verified?** Probably yes for identity — but a social account does not supply a phone number, so it does not automatically solve channel trust either.
4. **SMS costs money and has deliverability limits.** Who pays, and what is the fallback when it fails?

## Fix direction

Keycloak already provides the machinery — required actions, and TOTP is present but dormant. Prefer configuring the identity provider over hand-rolling verification in application code; a hand-rolled OTP flow is a well-known source of security defects.

Note the split-realm design: staff (`jtoye-dev`) and customers (`jtoye-customers`) are separate realms with separate policies. A change to one is **not** a change to the other, and the customer realm is the one with no required actions at all.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] A recorded decision on scope — channel verification vs. login second factor, and which flows require it.
- [ ] **If phone verification is adopted:** an unverified number cannot receive a payment link, proven by attempting it.
- [ ] Social-login accounts are handled per the recorded decision, not by accident.
- [ ] Configuration is **injected, never literal** (GLOBAL_RULE_6), and the realm template stays the source of truth so a realm re-import does not silently revert it — a documented trap in this repo.
- [ ] The existing JWT-forgery protections stay green: `alg=none` in all case variants, RS256→HS256 confusion, JKU injection and `kid` traversal all still rejected. These are confirmed-good today and must not regress.
- [ ] Verified against a **real Keycloak**, not a mock — realm configuration is exactly the layer a mock cannot exercise.
title: UX-6: password signups have no second factor and no verified contact channel (item 11)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (items 8 and 10). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"Order doesn't go through any payment processing. It just confirms."*
> *"'Pay on collection' is not allowed. This is because people can order and refuse to collect. The correct implementation is if a user is coming through social media, phone call or pick up; then a payment link should automatically be sent to them via the telephone number they've called on, or social media channel they've engaged on."*

## Item 8 — the code exists; the configuration does not

`PublicStorefrontService:508-521`: when the payment provider is not configured, the order path **deliberately** falls back to cash-on-delivery, goes straight to `PENDING`, and sets `paymentMethod = "Cash on Delivery"`. The card path is live behind `paymentService.isConfigured()`.

So this is **not missing code**. It is the known empty-`STRIPE_API_KEY` state on every stack, which is separately recorded as gating Phase 30 entirely and as the reason a refund E2E stays deliberately skipped.

**That distinction matters for sequencing:** the first action here is obtaining test-mode keys and exercising the card path end-to-end — not writing payment code. The money path has never been executed against Stripe even in test mode, so **every assumption about it is unverified**, including the assumption that the existing code works.

## Item 10 — a policy change, and it is the substantive part

Today `FulfilmentType` is `DELIVERY | COLLECTION` only (`FulfilmentType.java:10,13`), and with no provider configured every order is effectively pay-later.

The owner's ruling: **pay-on-collection is not permitted**, because a customer can order and simply not collect, leaving the vendor with produced stock and no payment. This is a real vendor-protection rule, not a preference.

The proposed model instead:

- an order arriving via **social media, phone call, or walk-up/collection intent** triggers an **automatically issued payment link**
- delivered back through the channel the customer engaged on — the phone number they called from, or the social channel they messaged on
- so the order is paid before production, whatever the channel

**Dependencies, stated plainly:** this needs the payment provider configured (item 8), and channel-return needs the messaging seam. A WhatsApp webhook seam exists from Phase 22 but its inbound parser is incomplete, so treat channel delivery as unbuilt rather than nearly-there.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] **First**, with test-mode keys configured: a card order completes end-to-end and the ledger row matches the order to the penny. This is the falsification that the existing path works at all.
- [ ] An order cannot reach a produced/preparing state as pay-on-collection.
- [ ] A payment link can be issued for an order created outside the storefront, and paying it advances the order.
- [ ] The link is single-use and expires — a payment link is a bearer credential and must not be indefinitely replayable.
- [ ] The existing COD fallback is **removed or gated deliberately**, not left as a silent default. It is currently what makes the policy violable.
- [ ] Every step verified against real Stripe test mode; a mocked provider would pass over exactly the integration this issue exists to establish.
- [ ] No live key is ever committed or logged — `gitleaks` and secret-scanning push protection stay green.

title: UX-5: orders complete with no payment, and pay-on-collection must be replaced by channel-issued payment links (items 8, 10)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (item 7). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"No sign of user/device location being utilised. Yet location/address is extremely important. It defines where the food is going to, what vendors a user has access to, and what vendors exist but are not near enough for delivery service. Someone in Birmingham should be able to see Birmingham vendors. London will be too far."*

## Verified — this is an absence, not a defect

Measured across `frontend/{app,components,lib,hooks}`, `core-java/src/main`, `edge-go/internal`:

| probe | hits |
|---|---|
| `navigator.geolocation` | **0** |
| `deliveryRadius` | **0** |
| `delivery_radius` | **0** |

- **Device location is never requested.** Anywhere.
- **Shop coordinates exist but are inert.** `PublicStorefrontService` puts `latitude`/`longitude` on the shop DTO (`:657-658`), and nothing computes a distance from them. There is no nearby/radius/within filter on the published-shops query.
- **Postcode is captured, not used geographically.** It is required for a delivery order and stored on it (`PublicStorefrontService:397-404`) — it answers *where this order goes*, never *which vendors you may see*.
- **Postcode "search" is a substring match.** `hero-search.tsx` searches name, description and address, so a postcode matches only if that literal string appears in a shop's address text. The file's own header comment records that this field previously *"promised… a postcode, and none of it did anything"*.

**There is no concept of locality in the product.** A customer in Birmingham and a customer in London see the same vendor list.

## Why this is re-ranked above the other findings from this session

Everything else reported on 2026-08-02 is a fix. This one is a **missing subsystem that the business model already assumes**, and several other items are downstream of it:

- "which vendors a user has access to" — the marketplace's core filter
- "vendors that exist but are too far to deliver" — a feasibility rule with no home today
- delivery fee logic, which today cannot vary by distance because distance does not exist
- the discoverability work (#447): local SEO and `LocalBusiness` JSON-LD are weakened when the product has no locality model

**This should be scoped as a phase, not worked as an issue.** Filed here so it is tracked and visible; the deliverable from it is a design, not a patch.

## Design questions to settle first

Deliberately unanswered — answering them by writing code would prejudge them:

1. **Device geolocation, postcode entry, or both?** Geolocation carries a permission prompt and a privacy obligation; postcode entry works without either and is what UK food ordering conventionally uses.
2. **What defines "near enough"?** A straight-line radius, a delivery-time estimate, or vendor-declared coverage areas. Vendor-declared is the least clever and probably the most correct — a vendor knows where they will actually deliver.
3. **What does a customer outside all coverage see?** An empty list is a dead end; "no vendors deliver to you yet" plus collection-capable vendors is a product.
4. **Does locality affect the storefront's public/SEO surface?** Per-locality pages are strong for local search but multiply the surface area.
5. **Where does it live** — `shops` gains coverage rules, or a new locality model?

## Acceptance criteria

Expressed as decisions first, since criteria written before the model is chosen would prejudge it:

- [ ] A recorded decision (ADR) covering the five questions above.
- [ ] **If a coverage model is adopted:** a customer in one locality does not see vendors that cannot serve them, proven with two genuinely distant fixtures — a same-city pair will pass under a broken radius and prove nothing.
- [ ] Delivery-address capture stays working — regression guard on behaviour that is correct today (V45).
- [ ] Any location a customer supplies is treated as personal data: retention and the existing GDPR erasure path (#84 / V42) accounted for, not bolted on afterwards.
- [ ] If device geolocation is used, refusal is a first-class path — a customer who denies the prompt must still be able to shop.

labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: UX-4: the product has no concept of locality — device location unused, shop coordinates inert, no delivery radius (item 7)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (item 6). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"New user signed in but basket is pre-populated with items picked earlier in the same browser for a given vendor. I think this is correct behaviour as it might have been the same user who did the selection before logging in. However, I need to check and confirm that this is not a situation where order items are crossing profiles."*

The instinct to check was right. Here is the precise answer.

## What is safe, and provably so

The basket **cannot cross shops.** `frontend/components/storefront/cart-provider.tsx`:

- storage key is `jtoye-cart-{shopSlug}` (`:33-35`)
- the stored payload carries its **own** `shopSlug` (`:62-63`)
- the parser **rejects a payload whose slug does not match** and returns undefined (`:57-61`)

That belt-and-braces guard is deliberate and already covered by tests. A stale key cannot surface another shop's basket.

It also cannot cross devices or browser profiles — `localStorage` is per-browser-profile by definition.

## What is not safe

**The cart is keyed to no customer identity at all, and nothing clears it on an auth change.**

`customerLogout()` in `frontend/lib/customer-auth.ts:94-98` removes four keys — the logged-in marker, the expiry, the tokens and the profile. **It does not touch `jtoye-cart-{slug}`.**

So on one shared browser: customer A fills a basket → signs out → customer B signs in → **B inherits A's basket.**

The cart *is* cleared after a successful order (`checkout/page.tsx:124`, `:338`), so this only bites when a basket is abandoned rather than ordered — which is the common case.

## Severity, stated honestly rather than escalated

- **Not** a server-side leak. No cross-tenant access, no RLS involvement, nothing leaves the device.
- The contents are **public catalogue data** — productId, title, price, image, category. No PII.
- Bounded to **one physical browser profile**.

So: a correctness and trust defect on shared devices (a household tablet, a counter device, a library machine), not a data breach. The realistic harm is customer B ordering and paying for items customer A chose.

The owner's read — that carrying a pre-login basket forward is *desirable* — is correct and should be preserved. The bug is that it is carried across an **identity change**, not that it is carried at all.

## Fix direction

Clear or re-key the cart when the authenticated identity changes. Preserve the anonymous→signed-in carry-forward, which is the behaviour customers expect; break the A→B carry-over, which nobody expects.

Note the sharp edge: "same person who was browsing anonymously" and "different person on the same device" are indistinguishable at sign-**in**. The reliable hook is sign-**out**, and/or comparing the identity present at sign-in against the one that last wrote the cart.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] After customer A signs out and customer B signs in on the same browser, B does **not** see A's basket.
- [ ] An **anonymous** basket built before signing in **is** still carried forward for that same session — the desirable behaviour must survive the fix. A change that clears the cart on every auth event would satisfy the first criterion and break the product.
- [ ] The existing cross-shop guard still holds — regression guard on a control that currently works.
- [ ] The post-order clear still works.
- [ ] Each asserted in a **real browser** across an actual sign-out/sign-in cycle; a unit test over the provider cannot exercise an identity change.
title: UX-3: basket survives a sign-out, so a second customer on the same browser inherits it (item 6)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (items 1a, 2, 3, 4). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"When signed in, Track my order is present even before any order is placed… it shouldn't be there as an external item outside of the signed in user's profile."*
> *"Track my order when signed in should only be present when there's been an order, and should be auto populated."*
> *"Track my order should engage users… the page should be animated… customer should only be notified [when] shopping… [has] now been dispatched."*
> *"'For operators' should not be visible in a customer signed in page/profile."*

## Verified

In `frontend/components/storefront/storefront-nav.tsx`, **only `My Orders` is gated on a session**:

| item | desktop | mobile | gated on `profile`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shops | `:97` | `:213` | no |
| **For operators** | `:100-105` | `:218-224` | **no** |
| **Track order** | `:106-112` | `:226-229` | **no** |
| My Orders | `:113-121` | `:230-239` | **yes** |

The comment at `:92-93` shows this was a deliberate choice — *"destination parity with the shared PublicHeader, including 'For operators' so the operator door is reachable from /shop"*. So this is a **decision to revisit, not an oversight**: the parity goal is real, and the fix should keep the operator door discoverable to people who are *not* signed in as customers rather than simply deleting the link.

## The four changes requested

1. **`For operators` off the signed-in customer surface.** A customer who has authenticated has self-selected; the operator pitch is now noise at best and confusing at worst.
2. **`Track order` should not be a standalone destination for a signed-in customer.** It belongs inside the profile — a signed-in customer's orders are already known to the system.
3. **Auto-populate tracking for a signed-in customer**, rather than asking them to type an order number the system already has.
4. **Tracking an order unrelated to the signed-in account should not be possible** except under a deliberately designed feature.

On (4) — worth knowing before scoping: the guest path is **already partly protected**. A guest-order deep link opened in a fresh browser context correctly demands the email before showing anything (verified in QA council `disc-20260802-121732`). So this is about the signed-in experience, not an open hole.

## Engagement and notifications (item 3)

Two separable pieces:

- **The tracking page should convey progress**, giving a sense of service level independent of a delivery ETA. Motion here is functional, not decorative — it answers "is anything happening?".
- **A dispatch notification.** The customer should be told when the order — cooked food or groceries — has been **dispatched**. Phase 22's notification layer already sends real email through the lifecycle (Received / Confirmed / Being Prepared / Ready / Completed, verified live in the council run), so this is likely a state-mapping and copy change rather than new infrastructure.

**Explicitly out of scope, per the owner:** courier/dispatch *tracking* integration. If that lands later, this design should not have to be undone to accommodate it.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `For operators` is not rendered in the signed-in customer nav, on **both** desktop and mobile — the mobile sheet is a separate code path and a desktop-only fix leaves it live.
- [ ] The operator door remains reachable for non-customers (the `:92` parity intent is preserved, not discarded).
- [ ] `Track order` is not a standalone nav destination for a signed-in customer; tracking is reachable from the profile.
- [ ] A signed-in customer's tracking view is populated without manual entry of an order number.
- [ ] A signed-in customer cannot view an order not associated with their account. Prove with a **real second account**, not by inspection.
- [ ] The guest tracking path keeps its existing email challenge — regression guard on a control that currently works.
- [ ] A dispatch notification is delivered on the dispatch transition, and **only** on it. Verified by reading the sink (MailHog), not by asserting the call was made.
- [ ] Motion respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
title: UX-2: signed-in customer nav shows For operators + Track order ungated; tracking should live in the profile and auto-populate (items 1a, 2, 3, 4)

body:
**Source:** owner observation during live use, 2026-08-02 (items 1b and 9). Verified against the tree before filing.

## Reported

> *"Track my order… takes you to a page where you're not signed in anymore if you click it."*
> *"Going back to home when logged in logs one out."*

## What is actually happening — the diagnosis differs from the symptom

**The session is almost certainly not being destroyed. The header simply never asks about it.**

- `StorefrontNav` — the component that renders the customer's name, the sign-out control and *My Orders* — is mounted **only** by `frontend/app/shop/layout.tsx:43`.
- `/` and `/track` render `PublicShell` → `PublicHeader` (`frontend/app/track/page.tsx:43`).
- **`PublicHeader` contains zero references to `getCustomerSession`.** It is session-blind by construction.

So navigating from `/shop/...` to `/` or `/track` swaps to a header that cannot display a signed-in state. To the customer that is indistinguishable from being logged out — and it will read as "this site logged me out", which is a trust defect even though no session was touched.

The customer session itself is a `localStorage` marker (`jtoye-customer-logged-in` + expiry) read by `isLoggedIn()` in `frontend/lib/customer-auth.ts:105-112`. Nothing in the navigation path clears it — `customerLogout()` is the only thing that removes those keys (`:94-98`), and it fires from an explicit button.

**This is one bug with two reported faces**, and it is far cheaper than the auth defect it appears to be.

## Not yet proven

I verified that `PublicHeader` never checks the session. I did **not** verify in a browser that the session survives the navigation. That distinction matters: if it turns out the session really is lost, this is a different and much more serious issue. **Confirm in a real browser before writing any fix** — and confirm it before anyone touches auth code on the strength of the symptom.

## Fix direction

Make the public header session-aware, so a signed-in customer stays visibly signed in across `/`, `/track` and the marketing surfaces. Reuse the existing seam (`getCustomerSession` / the `jtoye-customer-logged-in` marker) rather than introducing a second notion of session state — two sources of truth here is how this class of bug returns.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] **First, the falsification:** in a real browser, sign in, navigate to `/` and `/track`, and record whether the session persists. Capture the result either way — this determines whether the rest of these criteria are the right ones at all.
- [ ] A signed-in customer sees signed-in chrome on `/`, `/track` and the marketing surfaces, not only under `/shop`.
- [ ] Signing out from any of those surfaces works and is reflected everywhere.
- [ ] Session state comes from **one** source shared with `StorefrontNav` — asserted by the absence of a second independent check, not by inspection.
- [ ] Verified in a browser, not by asserting on props: this is a runtime rendering behaviour and a component test would pass over it.

title: UX-1: the public header is session-blind, so / and /track read as "logged out" (items 1b, 9)

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, finding **F-M6-CLS** (Medium). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/fe-findings.md#PERF-01`.

> **Filed because the council's adjudication omitted it.** Like `F-H6`, `F-M6` is in `findings.json` but **in no group in `plan.md`**. Caught by a coverage sweep over every finding ID.

> **RE-SCOPED 2026-08-04 to `/dashboard/staff` only.** Re-measured at the same declared profile before touching any code, 2 runs each: only one of the three routes still breaches. The other two are struck below rather than deleted, so the original numbers stay readable. Fixing a route that already meets the budget would produce an unfalsifiable "fix" — the acceptance criteria here require the pre-fix number to be reproduced first, and for `/` and `/competitive` it no longer can be.

## What

Cumulative Layout Shift **breaches the repository's own budget**, measured at the repository's own declared throttle profile — 390 px viewport, 4× CPU throttle, Fast 3G, budget `CLS < 0.1` as declared in `frontend/e2e/webhooks-webperf.spec.ts:37`:

| route | CLS (council, 2026-08-02) | CLS (re-measured 2026-08-04, 2 runs) | budget | in scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/dashboard/staff` | **0.1805** | **0.1805 / 0.1805** | 0.1 | **yes — still breaching** |
| ~~`/`~~ | ~~0.1213~~ | 0.0000 / 0.0000 | 0.1 | no — within budget |
| ~~`/competitive`~~ | ~~0.1040~~ | 0.0000 / 0.0000 | 0.1 | no — within budget |

The instrument was shown able to see a real shift on the same runs — `/dashboard/kitchen` reports **0.1471** — so the two zeros are a measurement of those routes, not a broken observer. `/dashboard/kitchen` is a **separate** breach that was not in the council's list and is not in this issue's scope.

## Why it matters

This is not an imported benchmark or an opinion about performance — **the project set this budget itself and `/dashboard/staff` exceeds it**, at nearly double, on a working surface a vendor returns to repeatedly.

## Fix direction

Reserve space for late-loading elements — explicit image dimensions and skeletons sized to their content. Note that `width`/`height` are already exposed on pipelined media (Phase 24 D-07), so part of this may be a matter of *using* data that already exists rather than adding it.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `/dashboard/staff` measures **CLS < 0.1** at the declared throttle profile.
- [ ] Measured at the **same 390 px / 4× CPU / Fast 3G profile** the finding used — a localhost-unthrottled measurement will pass regardless and proves nothing, which is the documented trap.
- [ ] The pre-fix number is reproduced first, so the improvement is falsifiable rather than asserted.
- [ ] No other route regresses past the budget — measure the set, not only the one.
- [ ] The existing budget in `webhooks-webperf.spec.ts` is **not relaxed** to accommodate the result. Moving the budget to meet the measurement would satisfy the letter of this issue and defeat its purpose.
title: QA-A/F-M6: CLS breaches the repo own 0.1 budget on 3 routes at the repo own throttle profile (unadjudicated by the council)

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, finding **F-H6-MANUALREVIEW** (High). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/fe-findings.md#LIFE-02`.

> **Filed because the council's adjudication omitted it.** `F-H6` appears in `findings.json` and in the report's prose summary, but **in no group in `plan.md`** — not A, not B, not C. It was found and then not routed. Caught by a coverage sweep mapping every finding ID against the filed issues; without that it would have existed only inside a gitignored file with no owner. Same class of miss as the ones this council was convened to find.

## What

The onboarding gate model includes a **`MANUAL_REVIEW`** state — an FHRS check that no automated rule can settle and that requires a human. The state exists in `vendor_onboarding_gate` and is reachable.

**It is rendered on no surface.** `/dashboard/onboarding/approvals` reports *"No applications waiting"* because it only surfaces checks that **PASSED**. An application sitting in `MANUAL_REVIEW` is invisible to everyone.

## Why this is a genuine dead-end, not a known limitation

This project has **no cross-tenant platform operator** — every admin surface is tenant-scoped, and that is a deliberate architectural decision, not an oversight. So the usual answer ("an operator console handles it") does not apply here, and the council explicitly flagged that: *"NOT the excluded operator console — this is a genuine dead-end."*

The result is a **two-actor continuity break**. The onboarding state machine is the sole writer of `Shop.published`. An application that lands in `MANUAL_REVIEW` therefore:

- cannot progress, because nobody can see it needs attention
- cannot publish the shop, because the state machine will not advance
- produces no notification, because nothing watches the state

The vendor sees an application that never resolves, with no indication anything is required of anyone. This is the same shape as the stalled-onboarding problem v2.3 was opened to fix.

## Fix direction

Surface `MANUAL_REVIEW` items on the tenant-scoped approvals page — the page already exists and already reads the gate table; it currently filters to PASSED only. Consider whether reaching the state should also notify, since a surface nobody visits is only marginally better than no surface.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] An onboarding in `MANUAL_REVIEW` appears on `/dashboard/onboarding/approvals`, with what is being asked stated.
- [ ] A human action from that surface moves the gate out of `MANUAL_REVIEW`, and the state machine can then progress the application.
- [ ] Proven **end-to-end from a real `MANUAL_REVIEW` row**, not from a mocked component — the defect is precisely that a real row renders nowhere, so a fixture-driven test could pass over it.
- [ ] The surface stays **tenant-scoped** — one tenant never sees another's applications. Prove with a real second tenant.
- [ ] A control arm confirms the assertion fails on the current build.
