title: QA-A/F-H6: onboarding MANUAL_REVIEW is on no surface — a genuine two-actor dead-end (unadjudicated by the council)

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, findings **F-H5-ONBOARD1** and **F-H7-NOINVITE** (both High) — their **structural halves**. Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/fe-findings.md#LIFE-01,LIFE-03`.

> **Filed because Group A's clustering covers only the copy.** The `small broken` cluster takes *"F-H5(a)"* — the inert switcher — and *"staff-invite copy → Keycloak reality"*. Both are interface corrections. The capability gaps underneath are real, are rated **High**, and would otherwise exist only inside a gitignored file. They need a product decision, which is why they are separate from the copy fix.

## Gap 1 — a multi-shop vendor can never take a second shop live (F-H5)

Onboarding is **one application per tenant**:

- `/onboarding/me` resolves through `VendorOnboardingRepository.findByTenantId`
- `OnboardingController` creates *"a DRAFT onboarding for the authenticated tenant"*
- a second attempt is refused with **409 — "an onboarding already exists for this tenant"**

The onboarding state machine is the **sole writer** of `Shop.published`. So a vendor who onboards one shop and later opens a second has **no path to publish it**. The shop can be created; it cannot go live.

This directly contradicts the multi-shop model the rest of v2.3 is built around — Phase 23 shipped per-shop staff scoping, and the dashboard carries a shop switcher throughout.

## Gap 2 — no staff-invite control exists (F-H7)

`/dashboard/staff` tells the operator to *"invite them to log in once"*, but **there is no invite control**, and the grant picker lists only the two already-authenticated users.

The binding constraint is D-09: `user_directory` is **populated at login**. So a user who has never logged in **cannot be granted access at all** — and there is no mechanism to prompt them to log in. Phase 23's headline journey cannot be *started* for any new user.

## Why these are filed together

Both are **lifecycle dead-ends**: the software models a state it provides no transition into. Both were found by walking the journey rather than testing an endpoint — each individual API works correctly.

Both also need the same kind of answer — a product decision, not a bug fix:

- Is onboarding **per-tenant** or **per-shop**? Per-shop is the larger change and probably the correct one, given every other v2.3 surface is shop-scoped.
- Is staff onboarding **invite-driven** (email an invite, provision on acceptance) or **login-first** (as today, with honest copy)? The login-first model is defensible; it is only broken because the UI promises otherwise.

## Acceptance criteria

Deliberately expressed as decisions first — writing code criteria before the model is chosen would prejudge it:

- [ ] A recorded decision on onboarding scope (per-tenant vs per-shop), with rationale. An ADR if it changes the model.
- [ ] A recorded decision on the staff-onboarding model.
- [ ] **If per-shop onboarding is adopted:** a second shop in an existing tenant can reach published, proven end-to-end; the state machine remains the sole writer of `published`; existing single-shop tenants are unaffected (migration path stated, not assumed).
- [ ] **If invite-driven staff onboarding is adopted:** a never-logged-in user can be granted access; `user_directory`'s login-population contract is either honoured or deliberately changed with the RLS implications restated.
- [ ] **If either is deliberately deferred:** the copy fix in the companion issue must be honest about the limitation — this issue is then closed as *decided*, not left implying a capability that does not exist.
title: QA-A/F-H5+F-H7: two lifecycle dead-ends — no 2nd-shop onboarding path, no staff invite (needs a product decision)

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, finding **F-M4-A11Y** (Medium) — the bulk of it. Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/a11y-findings.md`, `orchestrator-allergen-note.md`.

> **Filed because the council's own clustering does not place it.** Group A's `hand-rolled-modal` cluster claims *"F-M3, part of F-M4"*, and Group C routes the allergen text↔mask half to **#427**. The 419 violations are neither. Filing this rather than letting the largest single finding fall between two clusters — regression by omission is a defect here even when nothing is red.

## What

**419 axe violations across 27 routes**, desktop profile:

| severity | count |
|---|---|
| critical | 92 |
| serious | 221 |
| moderate | 103 |
| minor | 3 |

Dominated by two causes:

- **`color-contrast` — 220 violations**, across **at least 15 distinct failing colour pairs**. This is a design-token problem, not 220 separate bugs.
- **`button-name` — 92 violations**, essentially all **icon-only Edit/Delete buttons** in the dashboard. A screen-reader user hears "button" and must guess which one deletes.

**Mobile is not a subset of desktop** — `/competitive` goes 67 → **121** on mobile. Any fix verified only at desktop width will leave the mobile case unmeasured, and mobile is this product's primary profile.

Also recorded here: the allergen `<strong>` emphasis carries **no accessible allergen semantics**, and an unclosed `**` bolds to the end of the string. The *reconciliation* of allergen text against `allergen_mask` is **#427 / LGL-03 — do not double-file**; what belongs here is only that the emphasis is presentation-only.

## Why it matters

Accessibility is a standing contract in this project, and the 92 unnamed buttons are the sharpest item: they are **destructive actions** (Edit/Delete) with no accessible name, on the vendor's primary working surface.

The 220 contrast failures are the cheapest to fix disproportionately — 15 token pairs, not 220 sites — and they affect every user in sunlight on a phone, not only assistive-tech users.

## Fix direction

Two tractable passes, not a 419-item backlog:

1. **Contrast** — resolve the ~15 failing token pairs at the design-token level and re-measure. This should collapse most of the 220.
2. **Button names** — add accessible names to icon-only controls; likely one shared component.

Then re-measure and see what the genuine remainder is. Sequencing matters: fixing individual sites before the tokens means re-doing them.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `color-contrast` and `button-name` violations both reach **0** across the audited routes.
- [ ] Total violations are **measured and recorded** at both desktop **and mobile** widths — mobile is not a subset, so a desktop-only number is not evidence.
- [ ] The measurement is the **same axe sweep over the same 27 routes**, so the before/after numbers are comparable rather than a differently-scoped rerun.
- [ ] The baseline is captured **before** any fix, so the delta is falsifiable.
- [ ] Allergen emphasis carries real semantics, not `<strong>` alone; the unclosed `**` is fixed.
- [ ] No route regresses — a fix that improves 26 routes and worsens one is not done.

**Out of scope:** the storefront dish modal (separate issue) and allergen text↔mask reconciliation (**#427**).
title: QA-A/F-M4: 419 axe violations across 27 routes — 220 contrast pairs + 92 unnamed destructive buttons

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **small broken**. Findings **F-H5(a)**, **F-H7** (copy half), **F-L3-WHATSAPP**, **F-L6-PUBLISHDROP**, part of **F-L11-UXCOPY**. Council tier: LOW.

Grouped because each is a small, independent correction where the **system already behaves correctly and only the interface misrepresents it**. None requires a design decision.

> The deeper capability gaps behind F-H5 and F-H7 are **not** in this issue — the council scoped only the copy here. They are filed separately; see the companion issue.

## The items

**1. Onboarding shop-switcher is inert (F-H5(a))**
The shop switcher renders on the onboarding page but does nothing — the council measured marker 597→597 with **0 API calls**, against a control arm on `/products` that fired shopId-scoped calls correctly. Onboarding is per-tenant, so the switcher is meaningless there. **Hide it or honour it**; rendering a dead control is the one option that is wrong.

**2. Staff page promises an invite that does not exist (F-H7, copy half)**
`/dashboard/staff` says *"invite them to log in once"*, but there is no invite control and the grant picker lists only already-authenticated users. Make the copy describe what actually happens — the user must log in once before they can be granted.

**3. WhatsApp webhook returns 500 for a known unconfigured state (F-L3)**
Signing is not configured, and the endpoint fails **closed** — which is correct and **must stay**. But a *known* unconfigured state is not an internal error: it should be **503 with `Retry-After`**. Explicitly **not 501** — that would advertise the endpoint as unimplemented, which is wrong and worse.

**4. `PUT /shops` silently drops `published: true` with a 200 (F-L6)**
The onboarding state machine is the sole writer of `published` — that is correct and deliberate. But accepting the field, ignoring it, and returning 200 is unfalsifiable from the client's side. Reject it explicitly, or state in the response that it was not applied.

**5. UX copy defects (part of F-L11)**
- `"1 items"` pluralisation
- **duplicate DOM id** `shop-context-select` ×2 — invalid HTML, breaks label association
- **14 dashboard routes share one `<title>`**
- KDS *"All shops"* shows only one shop's tickets, silently
- `/dashboard/staff` ignores the shop switcher

## Why bother with LOW items

Each is individually trivial; together they are the texture a first-time vendor actually experiences. Two are correctness-adjacent rather than cosmetic — the duplicate DOM id is invalid HTML, and the KDS *"All shops"* filter **silently shows the wrong data**, which is a trust defect rather than a polish one.

## Acceptance criteria

Each written to **fail on the current tree**, verified per item:

- [ ] The onboarding switcher is either removed or fires shopId-scoped calls — asserted by API calls observed, not by the control rendering.
- [ ] Staff-page copy matches the login-populated `user_directory` reality.
- [ ] The WhatsApp unconfigured path returns 503 + `Retry-After`, and **still fails closed** (regression guard on a control that currently works correctly).
- [ ] `PUT /shops` with `published:true` no longer silently succeeds; the state machine remains the sole writer.
- [ ] Pluralisation correct; the duplicate DOM id is gone; dashboard routes have distinct titles; KDS "All shops" shows all granted shops or says which it is showing.
title: QA-A/small-broken: five interface corrections where the system is right and the UI misrepresents it

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **docs-onboarding**, finding **F-M8-DOCS** (Medium, class `docs-broken`). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/int-docs-as-tested.md`, `stalled-run-disposition.md#MED-COMPOSE`.

## What

**17 docs-broken + 12 docs-stale** across the onboarding surface. These were found by *executing* the documented commands in a clean shell, not by reading them:

- **`DOCKER_QUICK_START.md:96-104` states the API-prefix rule EXACTLY INVERTED** — roughly **85 curl examples** 404 as written.
- **`scripts/run-app.sh:5` hardcodes a superuser DB user the validator rejects**, so the documented "start the backend" step **cannot start the backend**.
- **"no `.env` needed" is false** — there are 18 required variables.
- **Every human-typed credential in the docs is dead.**
- **README / SETUP / QUICK_START all use `docker-compose` v1, which is not installed** — only v2 (`docker compose`) exists here.

`mcp-server/README.md` is the **only** fully-surviving entry document.

## Why it matters — and why no gate caught it

**None of the 19 doc gates cover these files.** The existing gates check metric counts, citations and changelog coverage; nothing executes a documented command. So every one of these could rot indefinitely while the doc suite stayed green — the same structural blindness recorded elsewhere in this repo.

The impact is specifically **go-to-market**. An outside reader — a contractor, a partner, a buyer doing technical diligence — follows the first-run path and it fails at step one, with an inverted rule that makes ~85 examples wrong. Every other quality signal in this repo is invisible to someone who cannot start the app.

## Fix direction

Mechanical but broad: correct the inverted prefix rule, fix `run-app.sh`'s DB user, migrate `docker-compose` v1 → v2 across the entry docs, replace the dead credentials with the real (config-sourced) route, and correct the "no `.env` needed" claim.

**Worth considering alongside:** a gate that actually *runs* the documented quickstart. Prose rules have repeatedly failed here where executable checks have not.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] The documented quickstart **runs as written in a clean shell** — the whole path, executed, not reviewed.
- [ ] The API-prefix rule matches live routing, verified by issuing one of the documented curl examples and getting a non-404.
- [ ] `scripts/run-app.sh` starts the backend with the user it names.
- [ ] No entry doc invokes `docker-compose` v1.
- [ ] The `.env` requirement is stated accurately.
- [ ] Credentials are sourced from config, never literals (GLOBAL_RULE_6) — `gitleaks` and secret-scanning push protection stay green.
title: QA-A/F-M8: 17 docs-broken in the onboarding surface — the first-run commands fail as written

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **problem-detail**, findings **F-M5-PROBLEMDETAIL** (Medium) + **F-L1-A3** (Low). Council tier: LOW-MED (contract additive). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/be-findings.md#BE-03,BE-04`, `sec-findings.md#A3`.

## What

**F-M5 — the OpenAPI contract lies about errors.**
- `application/problem+json` appears **0×** in the served `/v3/api-docs`.
- **105 declared 4xx/5xx responses point at success DTOs** — the declared 404 on products claims it returns `ProductDto`.
- **8 of 9** GET-by-id 404s have no body at all.
- Only the Phase-22 webhook endpoints follow the house RFC 7807 convention live.

**F-L1 — a cross-tenant existence oracle.** `GET /orders/shop/{id}` for another tenant's shop returns **200 with an empty list** rather than 403/404. The distinction between "this shop has no orders" and "this shop is not yours" is exactly what an attacker enumerates.

These are clustered because the same change decides both: what a non-happy-path response *is*.

## Why it matters

`GlobalExceptionHandler` already returns correct RFC 7807 bodies for ~30 exception types — the runtime is largely right. **The published contract does not describe it.** An agent or generated client reading the spec is told a 404 returns a `ProductDto`, so it will try to deserialise one.

This is a standing design-time contract here: *"errors are typed/machine-parseable (RFC 7807, stable codes) not prose-only; the OpenAPI/machine-readable contract matches live responses."* Right now the second half is false in 105 places.

Note the coupling: **#434** added a new `409 .../errors/concurrent-modification` on the order-transition endpoints. That status should be declared as part of this work.

## Fix direction

Register the `ProblemDetail` schema, correct the 4xx/5xx refs to point at it, ensure bare 404s carry a typed body. For F-L1, decide deliberately between 403 and a non-disclosing 404 — **#433 set the precedent of a non-disclosing 404 for cross-tenant**, and consistency with it matters more than the choice itself.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `application/problem+json` is present in the served spec, and a declared 404 references `ProblemDetail` rather than a success DTO.
- [ ] The count of 4xx/5xx responses pointing at success DTOs is **0** — asserted by a count over the served document, and the assertion observed returning 105 first.
- [ ] Live GET-by-id 404s carry a typed body.
- [ ] The new 409 from #434 is declared.
- [ ] `GET /orders/shop/{id}` cross-tenant answers consistently with the #433 precedent, and a test pins which one it is.
- [ ] `OpenApiSnapshotTest` / the OpenAPI breaking-change gate updated **deliberately**, with the diff reviewed rather than regenerated blindly.
title: QA-A/F-M5+F-L1: OpenAPI has no ProblemDetail schema — 105 declared 4xx point at success DTOs

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **seo-public-surface**, findings **F-H8-ROBOTS** + **F-H9-SEOMETA** (both High). Council tier: LOW (additive). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/fe-findings.md#SEO-01,SEO-02,SEO-04`.

## What

The public storefront has effectively **no discoverability layer**:

- **`/robots.txt` returns 404.** There is no `app/robots.ts` and no `public/robots.txt`. Nothing points a crawler at the sitemap. (`sitemap.xml` returns 200 — that was the control arm, so the 404 is real and specific.)
- **Every storefront shares one title and one description** — `/shop` and all three `/shop/[slug]` pages agree on a single title across 4/4 cells.
- **No canonical, no Open Graph, no Twitter card.**
- **Zero JSON-LD** across **28 priced, allergen-tagged dishes** — no Product, Offer or LocalBusiness markup anywhere.
- Heading order is H1→H2→**H4**.
- The sitemap **omits all three shop pages** and advertises a **`localhost` base URL**.

## Why it matters

This is a standing design-time quality contract in this project, not a nice-to-have: *"any phase building or reworking a public/unauthenticated surface owns its discoverability… For J'Toye this is storefront reach → vendor revenue, not polish."*

The value proposition to a vendor is reach. A storefront that cannot be crawled, has no per-shop title, and publishes no structured data for 28 priced dishes delivers none. The JSON-LD gap is the sharpest: rich results for food items are exactly what a local-search user sees, and the data to populate them is already in the database.

The `localhost` sitemap base URL will also mislead any crawler that does find it — and is coupled to the unresolved production-domain decision recorded in HANDOFF.md §4.

## Fix direction

`app/robots.ts` pointing at the sitemap; per-page `generateMetadata` for title/description/canonical/OG; Product + Offer + LocalBusiness JSON-LD on shop pages; fix the sitemap base URL and coverage. All additive — no existing behaviour is displaced.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `/robots.txt` returns 200 and references the sitemap.
- [ ] Each shop page has a **unique** title, description and canonical — asserted across all shop pages, not one; a single-page check cannot detect "all pages share one title", which is the actual defect.
- [ ] Valid Product/Offer JSON-LD on dish content and LocalBusiness on shop pages, **parsed and schema-validated**, not merely present.
- [ ] The sitemap includes every shop page and uses a **configured** base URL — never a literal (GLOBAL_RULE_6); it must follow the production-domain decision rather than hardcode a guess.
- [ ] Heading order is hierarchical.
- [ ] Assertions read the **served HTML**, and each is observed failing on the current build first.
title: QA-A/F-H8+F-H9: public storefront has no discoverability layer — robots 404, one shared title, zero JSON-LD

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **hand-rolled-modal**, findings **F-M3-DIALOG** + the modal portion of **F-M4-A11Y**. Council tier: LOW (one component). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/a11y-findings.md`, `fe-findings.md#A11Y-01`.

## What

`frontend/components/storefront/product-detail-modal.tsx` is an overlay with none of the dialog contract:

- `role`, `aria-modal` and `aria-labelledby` are all **null**
- the first Tab lands **outside** the modal — no focus trap
- **Escape does not close it** (overlay count 2→2)
- the close button has neither text nor an accessible name
- no scroll lock, no initial focus

## Why this one and not the others

**It is the only hand-rolled overlay in the codebase.** The cart drawer and all three dashboard dialogs already use Radix and are correct. So this is not an accessibility programme — it is one component that did not use the pattern the repo already standardised on.

It is also the **worst possible one to have missed**: the highest-traffic consumer surface, and the one that displays **allergen data**. A screen-reader user who cannot escape the dialog, or who never hears it announced, is being failed on the exact screen where the legal duty to communicate allergens applies.

This was previously recorded as `MED-MODAL` in the stalled `.qa-council/20260713-152124` run and **still reproduces** — it has been open across two councils.

## Fix direction

Port to Radix Dialog. The pattern is already in-repo in four places; this is a port, not a design exercise.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"` present, with an accessible name wired to the dish title.
- [ ] Focus moves into the dialog on open and is **trapped** — Tab from the last element returns to the first.
- [ ] Escape closes it; focus returns to the trigger.
- [ ] Body scroll is locked while open.
- [ ] Verified **in a real browser**, not by reading JSX — every one of the above is a runtime behaviour, and a props assertion would pass over a broken one.
- [ ] Each assertion observed **failing** against the current component first.

**Out of scope:** the 419-violation a11y backlog (separate issue) and the allergen text↔mask reconciliation (**#427** / LGL-03 — the council explicitly says *do not double-file*).
title: QA-A/F-M3: storefront dish modal is the only hand-rolled overlay — no role=dialog, no focus trap, Escape does not close

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **raw-image-endpoints**, finding **F-H3-RAWIMG** (High). Council tier: **HIGH** (contract/design decision, coupled with the media pipeline). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/be-findings.md#BE-02`.

## What

Three legacy endpoints — `POST /products/{id}/images`, `/shops/{id}/logo`, `/shops/{id}/banner` — store the client's **raw bytes unchanged** and serve them back as canonical. Confirmed by sha256 identity on a 2.5 MB 3000×2400 JPEG: what went in came back byte-identical.

That is **867×** the size of the pipelined derivative, on a public storefront.

The singular `POST /products/{id}/image` endpoint is correct and does run the pipeline. So the codebase currently contains both the right and the wrong behaviour for the same job.

## Why it matters

This contradicts a **stated design decision**. Phase 24 shipped the copy-on-write `media_asset` model specifically so that raw uploads are never canonical: magic-byte sniffing, a decompression-bomb guard, decode verification, EXIF stripping, and a WebP derivative under a declared budget. These three endpoints bypass all of it.

Three consequences, in descending order of severity:

1. **Security** — the validation chain exists to stop hostile uploads. These endpoints skip it entirely.
2. **Privacy** — EXIF stripping is skipped, so uploaded photos may carry GPS coordinates onto a public storefront.
3. **Performance** — an 867× payload on a mobile-first consumer surface, against the repo's own Core Web Vitals budget.

Related but distinct: **F-M2** records that the WebP pipeline currently reaches **0 customers** because the live catalogue is all legacy JPEG. Fixing this issue does not retroactively fix the catalogue.

## Fix direction

Route the three through the same pipeline as `/image`, **or retire them**. Retiring is legitimate if nothing depends on them — check before assuming. The design decision to restate explicitly: *raw uploads are never canonical.*

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] Bytes uploaded to each of the three endpoints are **not** served back byte-identical — assert on a sha256 comparison, which is the check that currently fails.
- [ ] A WebP derivative is produced for each, with width/height exposed.
- [ ] EXIF is stripped — verified by reading the served object, not by trusting the pipeline.
- [ ] The reject arms behave as `/image` already does: non-image magic bytes and an oversized/bomb image are refused with the same typed RFC 7807 errors.
- [ ] If any endpoint is **retired** instead, its callers are identified first — by IDE call hierarchy, not grep, per the repo's standing note that text search cannot answer "is this still used".

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: QA-A/F-H3: three legacy image endpoints store raw bytes as canonical, bypassing the Phase-24 pipeline

body:
**Source:** QA council `disc-20260802-121732`, Group A, cluster **missing-tenant-guc**, finding **F-H4-WHDELIV** (High). Council tier: **HIGH** (RLS/tenant path). Evidence: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/int-findings.md#INT-01`.

## What

`GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}/deliveries` returns `totalElements: 0` under every filter **while the rows provably exist** — the council observed delivery rows with `attempt_count` 6 and genuine remote responses (405/503) in the database at the same moment the API reported none. Replay 404s for the same reason.

**The visible half of Phase 22 has never worked.** The retry half does: deliveries are attempted, backed off and auto-paused correctly. It is only the vendor's ability to *see* them that is broken.

## Root cause — one line, and it is a repo-wide pattern warning

`WebhookDeliveryController` is the **only** controller that injects a repository directly with no `@Transactional`. `TenantSetLocalAspect` pins the tenant GUC around transactional boundaries, so with no transaction the aspect never fires, the GUC is never set, and RLS correctly returns nothing.

The security model worked exactly as designed. The endpoint simply never told it who was asking.

## Why it matters

A vendor debugging a failing integration is shown an empty log and concludes nothing was ever sent — when in fact six attempts were made and the subscription was auto-paused. That is worse than no feature: it actively misleads.

It is also a **latent-pattern** finding. Any future controller that injects a repository without a transaction inherits this silently, and RLS makes the failure look like "no data" rather than an error.

## Fix direction

Add `@Transactional` (or an explicit GUC pin) to the read path so `TenantSetLocalAspect` fires. Consider whether a guard should make the no-GUC case *loud* rather than empty — an unpinned read returning zero rows is indistinguishable from a genuine zero, which is a documented trap in this repo.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] `GET /webhooks/{id}/deliveries` returns the rows that provably exist in the table for that tenant.
- [ ] Replay works on a delivery returned by that endpoint.
- [ ] **The test proves the instrument can see the rows before asserting on them.** A test written against an empty table passes whether or not this is fixed — the documented "RLS blinds the verification query" trap. Seed, confirm visible, then assert.
- [ ] Cross-tenant isolation still holds: another tenant's deliveries are **not** returned. Prove with a real second tenant, not by inspection.
- [ ] A control arm shows the assertion failing on the pre-fix code.

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: QA-A/F-H4: webhook delivery log is permanently empty — the visible half of Phase 22 never worked

body:
**Source:** QA council run `disc-20260802-121732`, Group B, finding **F-M7-C234** (Medium severity). Part of **SEC-02**, Phase 28.

> Deliberately sanitised — public repository. Endpoint inventory and reproduction detail: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/sec-findings.md#C2,C3,C4` (gitignored, local only).

## Read the scope first — this is the one that reaches production

The council rated this **Medium**, and the other four Group B findings **Critical/High**. That ordering is correct on severity and **misleading on urgency**, because the other four are explicitly dev-stack-only while **this one is not**.

The relevant `permitAll` entries in `SecurityConfig` are **not profile-gated**. They apply in every profile, including `prod`. The metrics endpoint, the OpenAPI document and the edge gateway's metrics endpoint are therefore unauthenticated on any deployed instance, not just locally.

Nothing is deployed today, which is the only reason this is not live exposure. That also makes it the cheapest possible moment to fix it — it is a deploy-blocker being closed before there is a deployment to block.

## Why it matters

- The metrics endpoint is a large document describing internal structure, traffic shape and per-endpoint volumes. Metrics are a well-established reconnaissance source: they leak route names, tenant activity levels and error patterns without a single authenticated request.
- The OpenAPI document exposes the full API surface — a substantial number of paths — unauthenticated, and per **F-H2** it also advertises a tenant-selection header it should not.
- The edge gateway's metrics endpoint is the same class of problem in a second runtime.

## Fix direction

Gate these behind authentication in non-development profiles, keeping them open in `dev` so local tooling, the Prometheus scrape and the existing alert gates keep working. The scrape path must keep working in **every** environment — a fix that authenticates the endpoint but does not give Prometheus a way in will silently blind the entire Phase 27 alerting layer, which is a worse outcome than the finding.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] Under a production profile, the metrics endpoint, the OpenAPI document and the edge metrics endpoint all require authentication.
- [ ] Under `dev` they remain open, and `scripts/check-alert-liveness.sh`, `check-alert-metrics.sh` and `check-alert-rules.sh` all still return rc=0.
- [ ] Prometheus can still scrape in the gated profile — proven by a **successful scrape**, not by the config declaring credentials. A structural check here would pass over a dead scrape, and the alerting layer would go quiet without anything turning red.
- [ ] Each assertion is observed **failing** against the current unfixed profile before it is trusted.

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: SEC-02/F-M7: actuator, OpenAPI and edge metrics are permitAll in ALL profiles — the one Group B finding that reaches prod

body:
**Source:** QA council run `disc-20260802-121732`, Group B, finding **F-H10-INFRAPORTS** (High). Part of **SEC-02**, Phase 28. Overlaps the previously-recorded pentest items B1/B2/C1.

> Deliberately sanitised — public repository. The port inventory and reproduction detail stay in `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/sec-findings.md#C1` (gitignored, local only).

## What

Every infrastructure service in the local Compose stack publishes its port **with no bind address**, so all of them listen on all interfaces. This is the general case of which F-C2 (Postgres) is one instance; this issue covers the remainder — the mail catcher, object storage, cache, broker management UI and identity provider.

The mail catcher is the sharpest of them: its API is unauthenticated by design, and it currently holds a body of captured outbound email — order confirmations and notification traffic carrying real customer names and addresses from the dev tenants.

**Not a finding, recorded so it is not "fixed" by accident:** the broker's management UI correctly **rejected** its default credentials. That is a control working. Any change here must leave it working.

## Scope

**Compose dev stack only.** The finding records that k8s already binds internally. This is a `docker-compose.full-stack.yml` change, not an application or manifest change.

## Why it matters

Individually these are development conveniences. Together they are a complete lateral-movement surface on whatever network the workstation joins: storage, cache, queue, identity and the mail archive, all reachable, with the mail archive requiring no credential at all.

The GDPR angle is real and independent of the security one — Phase 19/#84 went to some trouble over erasure completeness and address scrubbing, and an unauthenticated archive of every notification email is the same data by another route.

## Fix direction

Bind published infra ports to loopback / an internal network under a dev-only Compose profile. Keep the ports usable for local development — this should not make the stack harder to work with, or it will be reverted.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] No infra service in the Compose stack publishes on all interfaces.
- [ ] The mail-catcher API is not reachable from off-host.
- [ ] The scan is **enumerative** — it asserts over the full set of published ports discovered from Compose's own parse, not a hand-written list. A hardcoded list silently stops covering a service added later.
- [ ] The broker management UI still **rejects** default credentials afterwards (regression guard on a control that currently works).
- [ ] `scripts/start-dev.sh`, the Playwright suite and the `webapp-testing` flow all still work against the rebound stack — verified by running them, not by reasoning about them.
title: SEC-02/F-H10: all Compose infra ports published on all interfaces; mail archive unauthenticated

body:
**Source:** QA council run `disc-20260802-121732`, Group B, finding **F-H2-XTENANT** (High). Part of **SEC-02**, Phase 28. Overlaps the previously-recorded pentest item A2.

> Deliberately sanitised — public repository. Reproduction detail: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/sec-findings.md#A2` (gitignored, local only).

## What — two halves, and only one of them is dev-scoped

**Half 1 — the behaviour (dev-scoped).** `TenantFilter` supports a request-header tenant fallback. It is annotated `@Profile({"dev","local","test"})` and every k8s environment sets `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`, so the code path is **dead under production**. Compose runs `dev`, so it is live locally.

**Half 2 — the advertisement (NOT dev-scoped).** `OpenApiConfig.java:50` publishes that header security scheme **unconditionally**, and the OpenAPI document is served unauthenticated. So the machine-readable contract advertises a tenant-selection mechanism to anyone who fetches it, in every profile, including ones where the mechanism does not exist.

Half 2 is the part that survives to production, and it is the part most likely to be missed — it is a documentation defect with a security consequence, not a code path.

## Why it matters

An unauthenticated spec that advertises a tenant-override header is a map. It tells a reader which header to try, against a service where the answer in `dev` is "it works". It also misleads legitimate integrators: agent-readiness is a standing quality contract here, and a spec that does not match live behaviour is a broken contract regardless of the security angle.

## Fix direction

Stop advertising the scheme in the spec (profile-gate the `OpenApiConfig` registration, or drop it). Separately confirm no non-prod profile is ever reachable from an untrusted network. Phase 28's SEC-03 already scopes the spec half.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] The unauthenticated OpenAPI document does **not** advertise the header scheme under a production profile.
- [ ] The assertion is made against the **served document**, not the source file — a source grep cannot see what the running service renders.
- [ ] A control arm proves the assertion can fail: it must fire on the current, unfixed configuration.
- [ ] The `dev`/`local`/`test` profile gating on the filter itself is confirmed still present and **unchanged** — the fallback is deliberate for local development, and removing it is out of scope for this issue.
- [ ] `OpenApiSnapshotTest` / the OpenAPI breaking-change gate is updated deliberately, and the diff reviewed rather than regenerated blindly.

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: SEC-02/F-H2: unauthenticated OpenAPI advertises a tenant-override header scheme in every profile

body:
**Source:** QA council run `disc-20260802-121732`, Group B, finding **F-C3-GRAFANA** (Critical). Part of **SEC-02**, Phase 28.

> Deliberately sanitised — public repository. Reproduction detail: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/sec-findings.md#B2` (gitignored, local only).

## What

The Grafana instance in the local monitoring stack still accepts its **factory-default administrator credentials**, and its port is published on all interfaces rather than an internal network. Authentication succeeds; this was confirmed by an actual login, not inferred from configuration.

## Scope

**Local monitoring stack only.** Grafana is defined in `infra/monitoring/docker-compose.monitoring.yml`. It has no Kubernetes equivalent at all — `k8s/` ships **zero** monitoring manifests, which is separately tracked as DPLY-03.

That absence cuts both ways: there is no deployed Grafana to be exposed, and there is also no deployed Grafana at all, so the fix here should not be written in a way that has to be redone when the k8s manifests land.

## Why it matters

Grafana holds the operational view of the platform — dashboards over tenant order volumes, financial series and alert state. Administrative access also permits editing datasources, which in this stack means a direct query path to Prometheus.

Factory-default credentials are the single most-scanned weakness on any exposed service; this needs no skill to exploit.

## Fix direction

Set the admin credentials from configuration (environment/secret, never a literal — see the project's config rule), and restrict the published port to the internal network. Carry the same credential handling into the k8s monitoring manifests when DPLY-03 is built, so this is fixed once rather than twice.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree**:

- [ ] The factory-default credential pair is rejected by the running Grafana.
- [ ] The replacement credential is injected via configuration, with no literal in a committed file (`gitleaks` and the secret-scanning push protection must both stay green).
- [ ] The port is not published on all interfaces.
- [ ] The rejection is demonstrated **live against the running instance**, not asserted from the config file — a config assertion can pass over a container that never reloaded it. (See the project's standing note on structural checks passing over dead features.)

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: SEC-02/F-C3: local Grafana still accepts factory-default admin credentials, port published on all interfaces

body:
**Source:** QA council run `disc-20260802-121732`, Group B, finding **F-C2-PGSUPER** (Critical). Part of **SEC-02**, Phase 28.

> Deliberately sanitised. This repository is public, so the reproduction steps, the bound address/credential pairing and the role attributes stay in the local evidence file rather than here. Full detail: `.qa-council/disc-20260802-121732/evidence/sec-findings.md#B1` (gitignored, local only).

## What

The Postgres container in the **local Compose dev stack** publishes its port with no bind address, so it listens on all interfaces rather than the loopback/internal network. The account reachable there holds role attributes that bypass row-level security, which means tenant isolation — the platform's primary security boundary — does not apply to a connection made that way.

## Scope — read this before prioritising

**Dev stack only.** The finding explicitly records that staging/production already bind internally, and `k8s/` is unaffected. The exposure is on a developer workstation, and its severity depends entirely on what network that workstation is attached to.

This is *not* a statement that the deployed configuration is wrong. It is a statement that the local one is, and that the local one is where every developer's real tenant data sits.

## Why it matters beyond the dev box

RLS is enforced at the database. Every other layer — `TenantContext`, the JWT filter, `ShopAccessService` — assumes the database will refuse a cross-tenant read even if the application layer is wrong. A connection that bypasses RLS removes the backstop that the whole design leans on. It is worth closing on the dev stack precisely because that is where the assumption gets casually tested.

## Fix direction

Bind the published port to the internal network / loopback under a dev-only Compose profile, and rotate the credential. No application code change.

## Acceptance criteria

Written to **fail on the current tree** — verify by running them before the fix and confirming they fail:

- [ ] The Postgres service publishes on loopback or an internal network only; a bind-address scan of the running stack shows no all-interfaces binding for it.
- [ ] The credential in use has been rotated.
- [ ] The check is executable and observed **failing** against the pre-fix configuration, not only passing after — a bind-address assertion that has never fired is not evidence.
- [ ] `k8s/` and the staging/production overlays are confirmed **unchanged** by the fix (they were already correct; a change there would be a regression, not a fix).

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Critical before first real tenant — security & correctness gate

title: SEC-02/F-C2: dev-stack Postgres port published on all interfaces, reachable by an RLS-bypassing role

body:
## Problem

Customer storefront signup/login is **username + password only**. There is no social signup
(Google / Apple / Facebook), which is checkout-conversion friction on a consumer surface.

## Measured on the tree (2026-08-02, HEAD 39678c6e)

- The storefront uses its own identity realm, `jtoye-customers`, via a PKCE authorization-code
  flow in `frontend/lib/customer-auth.ts` (`response_type: code`, `code_challenge_method: S256`),
  with the callback at `frontend/app/shop/auth/callback/page.tsx`.
- **`identityProviders: 0`** in all four realm artifacts — `infra/keycloak/realm-export-customers.json`,
  `realm-export-customers.template.json`, `realm-export.json`, `realm-export.template.json`.
- No `kc_idp_hint` anywhere in the repo, so no deep-link to a provider exists either.
- The vendor dashboard (`frontend/auth.ts:51`) configures exactly one NextAuth provider,
  `Keycloak({...})` — noted for completeness; **this issue is scoped to the storefront only.**

## Why this is filed rather than just fixed

It was invisible to every review process: **zero** mentions in `.planning/REQUIREMENTS.md`,
**zero** in `.planning/ROADMAP.md`, and no open or closed issue. That is the same structural
blindness recorded in `HANDOFF.md` §0.1 — work with no phase, no requirement ID and no ticket
cannot be seen by a roadmap- or tracker-driven review. This is the third instance
(after ADR-0004's ingredient graph → #427, and the catering cohort → #428).

## Scope

Storefront customer identity only. Explicitly **not** vendor/staff login — that path touches
`shop_staff` JIT provisioning and the strict-scoping switch, and changing it has tenant-isolation
consequences.

## Acceptance criteria

Each must be capable of FAILING on the tree as it stands today.

1. At least one external identity provider is configured on the `jtoye-customers` realm, present
   in the **committed template** (not only in a live realm — a live-only change is lost on
   re-import; see the realm re-import trap where a volume drop is a no-op because Keycloak is
   Postgres-backed). Fails today: `identityProviders` is `[]` in every artifact.
2. The storefront sign-in surface offers the provider, and a real end-to-end browser run reaches
   an authenticated storefront session — a Playwright journey, not a rendered button. Per repo
   standard, asserting the button exists is not evidence; click it and verify the outcome.
3. A customer who signs up socially can complete checkout, and the resulting order carries the
   same customer linkage as a password signup. Falsifiable by comparing the persisted rows.
4. The provider's client secret is injected as configuration, never committed — consistent with
   the existing sealed-secret handling.
5. CSP permits the provider origin. Recorded prior art: a CSP source **with a path** matches
   exactly unless it ends in `/`, which previously blocked customer sign-in while the realm URL
   was listed in the directive.

## Open decisions (not engineering tasks)

- **Which providers.** Google alone is the cheapest meaningful slice for a UK food-ordering
  consumer; Apple is required by App Store policy only if a native iOS app ships, which is not
  on the roadmap.
- **Account linking.** Whether a social identity that matches an existing password account's
  email auto-links or is rejected. Keycloak's default is a first-broker-login flow; picking
  wrong here is an account-takeover vector, so it needs a recorded decision rather than a default.
- Data-protection posture: a social provider returns profile data the platform does not
  currently collect. Relates to the LGL-01 retention policy.

## Suggested placement

New requirement in `.planning/REQUIREMENTS.md`. Phase 31 (Consumer-Safety and Legal Floor) is the
natural home given the account-linking and data-protection decisions, but it is a conversion
feature rather than a legal floor, so it may warrant its own slice.
title: Customer storefront has no social signup — jtoye-customers realm has identityProviders: 0

body:
## Why this issue exists

**The go-to-market names two cohorts. Only one of them has a product, and the other has never had a
tracker entry.** `docs/analysis/BUSINESS_MODEL_DECISION_GUIDE.md` sets the target as *"established,
owner-led Nigerian and West African food operators in one dense city cluster"*, and is explicit:
*"Treat takeaway and catering as separate discovery cohorts."* Catering is positioned as the wedge —
*"Catering/pre-order as a wedge … deposits, amendments, quantities, and timed fulfilment have
attributable value"* — and as *"an equal discovery priority"*.

That thread lives only in an analysis document. It has no phase, no requirement ID and no issue, so
every roadmap- or tracker-driven review has missed it (confirmed during the 2026-08-01 state review).
This issue is its tracker representation. Companion: the ADR-0004 ingredient-graph epic, missing for
the same structural reason.

## Current state — measured 2026-08-01

**Cohort B has zero implementation.**

- No Quote, Enquiry, Booking or Catering entity anywhere in `core-java/src/main`
- `fulfilment_type` is `DELIVERY | COLLECTION` only (V45) — there is no pre-order, event-date or
  timed-fulfilment seam
- No deposits, amendments, headcount capture, cut-offs, production lists or cancellation rules

**What is shipped is the honesty, and it is worth protecting.** The live `/for-operators` page
already tells operators, in writing, that *"Catering and WhatsApp are validation tracks. They are not
current, guaranteed production workflows"* — see
`frontend/components/marketing/operator-pitch.tsx:114` and `:130`, which carries the same disclaimer
for connected-account settlement. The fit-check widget offers Takeaway / Catering / Both and produces
a local summary only, with no lead capture.

**Nothing in this epic may weaken those disclaimers ahead of the capability.** If a workflow ships,
the disclaimer changes with it, in the same PR.

## The stance this epic takes — discovery before build

The business-model guide calls these **discovery** cohorts and rates the catering-wedge confidence
as *Medium*, with the open question recorded as *"complete workflow coverage and willingness to
pay"*. It also warns: *"Do not combine restaurants, home caterers, market stalls, and grocers into
one persona."*

So this epic is deliberately **gated, not scheduled**. Building quotation/deposit/production-list
workflow before a caterer has paid for it would be the most expensive way to answer a question that
interviews answer for free — and the guide's own framing says so.

**Gate to open Wave 2:** at least 3 catering operators interviewed against the Cohort B workflow
list below, with a recorded willingness-to-pay signal and at least one operator's real event
paperwork captured. Until then Wave 2 stays closed and no catering schema is written.

## Waves

**Wave 1 — discovery, no code (open now)**
- [ ] Interview ≥3 caterers against the Cohort B workflow list; capture real event paperwork
- [ ] Establish which cohort pays and retains better — the guide's stated open question
- [ ] Decide whether catering is one account alongside takeaway or a distinct journey. Working
      assumption already published on `/for-operators`: *"One account can support both, but neither
      journey should be flattened into the other"*
- [ ] Record the outcome as an ADR, so the answer is not re-litigated

**Wave 2 — P2, minimum catering slice (BLOCKED on Wave 1's gate)**

Scope named here so discovery has something concrete to test, **not** as a build commitment:
- [ ] Enquiry / quotation capture
- [ ] Deposits and cancellation rules (intersects Stripe Connect, #102 tenant lifecycle, and the
      currently-unexercised money path — no test-mode Stripe keys exist on any stack today)
- [ ] Headcount and quantity amendments with a cut-off
- [ ] Timed fulfilment — the `fulfilment_type` enum extension, and the first real reason to have one
- [ ] Production lists for the kitchen

**Wave 3 — P3, compounding (BLOCKED on Wave 2 and on the graph epic)**
- [ ] Ingredient purchasing and production-list expansion. This is where catering and ADR-0004 meet:
      the Ingredient node is what turns a production list into a purchasing list. Sequence after the
      graph epic's Wave 2, never before

## Explicitly out of scope

Marketplace, delivery operation, payment custody, merchant of record, complete POS, accounting
system, compliance guarantor — all excluded by the business-model guide's recommendation and not
reopened here.

## Definition of done for the epic

Either (a) a paying catering operator runs a real event end-to-end on the platform and the
`/for-operators` disclaimer has been updated in the same change that earned it, or (b) discovery
concludes catering is not the wedge and this epic is closed with that finding recorded in an ADR.
**Both are successful outcomes.** Closing this epic on "we built the features" without (a) would be
the failure mode.

## Related

Business-model source: `docs/analysis/BUSINESS_MODEL_DECISION_GUIDE.md`; cohort evidence in
`docs/audit/sources/08-market-analyst.md` and `09-vertical-saas-strategist.md`. #102 (tenant
lifecycle / billing / payouts — deposits depend on it), #61 (refund E2E, blocked on Stripe test
keys), #208 (WhatsApp — the guide's other named validation track, same disclaimer), and the ADR-0004
ingredient-graph epic.
title: [CATER-0] EPIC: Cohort B (catering) — discovery-gated product track

body:
## Why this issue exists

**ADR-0004 was Accepted on 2026-07-30 and has no phase, no requirement ID and no issue.** It was
authored as a `/gsd-quick` task (`.planning/quick/260730-kg1-adr-0004-knowledge-graph-strategy/`),
so any review driven by `ROADMAP.md` + `REQUIREMENTS.md` + the issue tracker misses it completely —
which is exactly what happened during the 2026-08-01 state review. This issue is the tracker
representation. Companion: the catering-cohort epic, missing for the same structural reason.

Source of truth stays `docs/architecture/decisions/ADR-0004-knowledge-graph-strategy.md` (468 lines).
Nothing here supersedes it; this issue schedules it.

## The decision, restated

**Adopt the graph data model. Reject the graph datastore.** A relational graph inside the existing
PostgreSQL — ingredient/edge tables, recursive CTEs for depth-bounded traversal, existing GIN/FTS,
pgvector (#207) for fuzzy matching.

Two rejections worth carrying forward, because both are repo-specific rather than generic:

- **Apache AGE is disqualified by our own RLS guard.** AGE creates label tables dynamically at
  graph-write time in a **per-graph schema**, and `RlsContractTest`'s sweep filters
  `relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace` (verified 2026-08-01 at
  `core-java/src/test/java/uk/jtoye/core/security/RlsContractTest.java:130`). AGE's tables would be
  **structurally invisible to that sweep** — the RLS drift guard would stay green over an
  unprotected graph. That is Proof Standard #5 reproduced in the subsystem where it is least
  affordable. Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server also lists AGE among the extensions that
  block in-place major-version upgrades.
- **A dedicated graph database is worse on the same axis.** Multiple databases and fine-grained
  access control are Neo4j Enterprise features. Either edition means re-implementing tenant
  isolation in application query-building — moving this platform's strongest invariant from
  *enforced by the database* to *intended by the application*. FORCE RLS proven under a NOSUPERUSER
  downgrade is not a property to spend.

## Current state — measured 2026-08-01

The **edges** largely exist as shipped columns: `Customer.allergenRestrictions` and
`Product.allergenMask` (same bit space), `OrderItem.productId`, `Product.shopId`, `Shop.latitude` /
`longitude`, `Review`, the onboarding `BUSINESS_VERIFIED` / `FOOD_HYGIENE_RATING` gates, and
`media_asset (tenant_id, sha256)`.

The **node does not**. `ingredients` is still free text (V1 / V25 / V41); there is no ingredient
table and no edge table in any migration. `Product.category` and `Product.dietaryTags` are free
strings, so there is no taxonomy either.

## The load-bearing gap — read this part even if the rest waits

**Nothing in the codebase ever reconciles `allergen_mask` against the ingredients text sitting in
the adjacent column.** The mask is an integer a vendor hand-types into a CSV column
(`BulkImportService` template header), and it is what the storefront renders — verified 2026-08-01
at `frontend/components/storefront/product-detail-modal.tsx:65`. Every allergen statement this
platform makes to a consumer resolves to that unverified field.

ADR-0004 also records that the guest-checkout allergen cross-check was **removed** (special category
data over an unauthenticated endpoint with no Article 9 condition — see
`docs/legal/article-9-allergen-basis.md`). So there is currently **no consumer-allergen matching at
checkout at all**, which is the correct position until a consented path exists.

Any re-introduction of consumer allergen matching is a **lawful-basis design question before it is a
code question.** Do not treat Wave 1 below as purely technical.

## Waves

Priority is **not** uniform across this epic. Wave 1 is a pre-first-tenant correctness concern (P1);
Waves 2–3 are P2; Waves 4–6 are P3 or commercial-gated. File children at their own priority.

**Wave 1 — P1, zero infrastructure, existing data only**
- [ ] Establish the lawful basis for consulting a stored customer allergen profile at checkout
      (authenticated path only), or record explicitly that we will not
- [ ] Order-level allergen mask aggregation
- [ ] Surface allergen conflicts on the KDS
- [ ] Onboarding critical-path traversal — the gates already form a DAG

**Wave 2 — P2, the unlock; worth its own phase**
- [ ] Layer B + the Ingredient node + a vendor-facing discrepancy queue reconciling declared
      `allergen_mask` against parsed ingredients text. **Advisory-only** — errors sit on a path with
      legal consequence, which caps achievable automation by design

**Wave 3 — P2, highest commercial return on this list per the ADR**
- [ ] The shopping-basket sense. Needs no schema change: `durabilityType='BEST_BEFORE'` plus
      `quantityInStock` already model an ambient grocery item. The work is UI, ingredient links and
      fulfilment/postage; the reward is a vendor catalogue no longer capped by delivery radius

**Waves 4–6 — P3 / gated**
- [ ] Substitution and dietary traversals; a graph-backed MCP `find_products` that answers safety
      constraints **structurally**, never letting a language model decide whether a dish contains milk
- [ ] The recipe sense, together with the unmet JSON-LD / `robots.txt` contract — vendor-authored,
      graph-assisted, never auto-published
- [ ] Supply chain **only** if a vendor-side capture mechanism materialises

## Accepted costs (from the ADR — do not rediscover these)

Ontology maintenance is perpetual and is what kills projects of this kind. Ingredient extraction from
free text has a long tail. Recursive CTEs are less expressive than Cypher (accepted; traversals are
depth-bounded). Layer B is a genuinely new plane to operate even without a new engine. Licence
containment (ODbL) and the Layer A / Layer B split are specified in the ADR and are **not** optional.

## Definition of done for the epic

A consumer-facing allergen statement is backed by evidence the platform can check, not solely by a
hand-typed integer — with the reconciliation advisory, the tenant wall unchanged (FORCE RLS on every
new table, swept by `RlsContractTest`), and no new datastore, isolation mechanism, backup surface or
upgrade constraint introduced.

## Related

ADR-0002 (managed vs manifest datastores — still `Proposed`, needs owner sign-off), ADR-0003 (the
precedent for rejecting a second datastore that dilutes the tenant wall), #207 (pgvector spike,
open), #209 (AI readiness — the MCP tool in Wave 4 inherits that epic's agent-readiness contract).

body:
Split out of #404, which was closed once its three remaining **failure** classes were fixed (#416). Two things it raised were never addressed, and would otherwise disappear with it.

## 1. CI runs `e2e/public-layout.spec.ts` only — 2 of 128 tests

The other 12 specs need a full stack (core-java + Keycloak + Postgres + MinIO + RabbitMQ) that the CI runner does not have. This is structural, not an oversight — but the consequence is that **126 of 128 E2E tests never run on any PR**, and #404 is the record of what that costs: a broken customer sign-in shipped and sat undetected because the suite that would have caught it was itself broken and unwatched.

Options worth weighing rather than assuming:
- run the compose stack in CI for a nightly (not per-PR) full-suite job;
- or a per-PR subset that needs only the frontend, extending the existing stack-free browser gate (#265);
- or accept the gap explicitly and gate on something else — but say so in writing, because right now the gap is implicit.

## 2. 14 tests SKIP rather than pass, and nothing reports the difference

Measured on the merged tree 2026-08-01: **114 passed, 14 skipped, 0 failed** of 128. Playwright's summary is green and a reader takes "0 failed" as "everything is verified". It is not.

The 14 are 7 distinct tests × 2 projects:

| spec | why it skips |
|---|---|
| `marketing-motion` ×2 | desktop-only GSAP scenes running under the **mobile** project |
| `stomp-relay` ×2 | needs multi-replica cross-replica broadcast |
| `vendor-refund-flow` ×4 | needs a refundable order in the dev DB |
| `storefront-flows` ×2 | needs a promotion/discount fixture |
| `onboarding-blocked-flow` ×2 | onboarding fixture |

**A skip is not a pass.** These are exactly the shape of the problem #404 was opened about — a green summary over surface nobody is actually checking. Two of them are cheap to convert now that `scripts/seed-media-review-fixtures.sh` establishes the pattern: seed the fixture with relative timestamps rather than skipping.

The `marketing-motion` pair is different and arguably a **spec bug**, not a missing fixture: a desktop-only scene should not be enumerated under the mobile project at all, so it should be a project filter rather than a runtime skip.

## Suggested first step

Make the skip count **visible and bounded** — fail the run if skips exceed a declared budget, so a new conditional skip cannot silently join the 14. That is the same shape as the anti-vacuity guard in `media-review-320.spec.ts`, which is the only reason its own decay was ever noticed.

Refs #404, #416.
title: E2E coverage gap survives #404: CI runs 2 of 128 specs, and 14 tests SKIP rather than pass

body:
`PaymentEventOutboxReliabilityIntegrationTest > retry-exhausted FAILED rows resurrect to PENDING and drain; poison rows stay FAILED` fails non-deterministically and **blocks merges**, because `Integration Tests (Testcontainers RLS)` is a required check.

## It is a race, not a defect — it fails in BOTH directions

Observed on 2026-08-01 on two **unrelated** branches, at the **same line**, with **opposite** Mockito errors:

| PR | branch touches | error at `PaymentEventOutboxReliabilityIntegrationTest.java:273` |
|---|---|---|
| #415 | `CorsConfig` only | `org.mockito.exceptions.verification.TooManyActualInvocations` |
| #417 | `RateLimitInterceptor` only | `org.mockito.exceptions.verification.WantedButNotInvoked` |

Neither branch touches the payment or outbox path. A real defect fails in one direction; **failing in both is the signature of a timing race.**

## Mechanism

The assertion is:

```java
flusher.flushPending();
verify(rabbitTemplate, times(1)).convertAndSend(anyString(), anyString(), any(Object.class));
```

`flushPending()` is **also a live scheduled method** in the same context:

```java
@Scheduled(fixedDelayString = "${payment.outbox.flush-interval-ms:5000}")
public void flushPending() { ... }
```

The test is a plain `@SpringBootTest` with **no** property lowering/disabling that schedule, and the background scheduler shares the very same `@MockBean RabbitTemplate` the assertion counts. So every 5 seconds the scheduler independently drains the outbox against the mock:

- scheduler fires **before** the explicit call → the row is already `SENT`, the explicit call sends nothing → **`WantedButNotInvoked`**
- scheduler fires **around** the explicit call → two sends → **`TooManyActualInvocations`**
- scheduler misses the window → exactly one → **passes**

## Why it surfaced now

Both failing runs were slow and contended — 41m and 46m, carrying **500** and **477** `Connection refused` / `connection has been closed` lines from starved Testcontainers Postgres instances. A loaded runner widens the window between the row becoming `PENDING` and the explicit `flushPending()`, so the 5-second scheduler lands inside it. The **identical SHA** of #415 passed this job in an earlier, uncontended run — which is what makes "it's the tree" untenable.

## Suggested fix (not applied here — out of scope of the PR that found it)

Push the background schedule out of the test's lifetime rather than sleeping or loosening the assertion:

```java
@TestPropertySource(properties = {
    "payment.outbox.flush-interval-ms=3600000",
    "payment.outbox.resurrect-interval-ms=3600000"
})
```

`times(1)` then means what it says: exactly one send, caused by the explicit call.

**Please check the sibling suites before closing** — `MediaEventOutboxFlusher` was cloned from this flusher and any test that calls a `@Scheduled` method directly while asserting invocation counts on a shared mock has the same shape.

**Do not "fix" this by relaxing to `atLeast(1)`.** The exactly-once count is the property under test: the whole point of the outbox is that a resurrected row drains once and the poison row is never republished. Loosening it would leave a green test over the behaviour it exists to protect.

Found while landing #412/#413 (PRs #415, #417).
title: Flaky required check: PaymentEventOutboxReliabilityIntegrationTest races its own @Scheduled flusher

body:
Found while fixing #409 (PR #410). Split out because it changes a live API response contract.

## The defect

CLAUDE.md's standing **AI agent-readiness** contract requires that *"errors are typed/machine-parseable (RFC 7807, stable codes) not prose-only"*, and the codebase honours that everywhere else — `GlobalExceptionHandler.java:52-54` builds a real `ProblemDetail`:

```java
ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
problem.setTitle("Resource Not Found");
problem.setType(URI.create("https://jtoye.uk/errors/not-found"));
```

`RateLimitInterceptor` bypasses that entirely and writes JSON by hand, in **two** places:

- `RateLimitInterceptor.java:158` (tenant path) — `{"error":"Too Many Requests","message":"Rate limit exceeded. Please try again in %d seconds.","tenantId":"%s"}`
- `RateLimitInterceptor.java:258` (public path) — same minus `tenantId` (deliberately, so a guest request leaks none)

So the one field every other error surface uses — `detail` — is absent, and the wait is only available as **prose inside `message`**.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

It already cost real behaviour. The checkout read `response.data.detail`, correctly following the documented contract, and got nothing — so a rate-limited shopper was told *"Failed to place order. Please try again."*, which is the exact action that re-trips the limit (#409). The fix in #410 had to special-case the non-7807 shape.

An agent or client written against the documented contract sees a 429 with **no `detail`**, and has to know this one endpoint family is different. That is precisely what the contract exists to prevent.

## Proposed fix

Emit `ProblemDetail` from both paths, matching the existing precedent, and carry the wait as a **typed field** rather than only prose:

```java
ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
    HttpStatus.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS, "Rate limit exceeded. Please try again in " + waitForRefill + " seconds.");
problem.setTitle("Too Many Requests");
problem.setType(URI.create("https://jtoye.uk/errors/rate-limited"));
problem.setProperty("retryAfterSeconds", waitForRefill);
```

Keep the public path free of `tenantId` — that omission is deliberate and load-bearing.

## ⚠ Coordinate with the frontend, or #409 silently regresses

`frontend/lib/order-error.ts` currently recovers the wait by parsing `data.message` with a narrow regex, because `Retry-After` is invisible cross-origin (#412). **Changing `message` → `detail` without updating that helper will drop the quantified copy back to the vague "wait a moment"** — no test would fail on the server side, and the frontend unit tests construct their own fixtures, so nothing goes red. Ship them together, or land #412 first so the header path works and the body parser stops mattering.

Known consumers of the current shape:
- `frontend/lib/order-error.ts` + `frontend/lib/__tests__/order-error.test.ts`
- `core-java/src/test/java/uk/jtoye/core/security/RateLimitInterceptorTest.java`
- `core-java/src/test/java/uk/jtoye/core/security/RateLimitIntegrationTest.java.disabled`

## Acceptance criteria — each must be shown to FAIL first

1. A throttled response validates as RFC 7807: `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` all present, `Content-Type: application/problem+json`. **Fail direction:** assert against the current hand-rolled body and confirm the check goes red — do this before the change, so the assertion is proven capable of failing.
2. The public path still emits **no** `tenantId`. **Fail direction:** plant one and confirm the test catches it. This must not regress while reshaping the body.
3. `retryAfterSeconds` is a typed number equal to the `Retry-After` header value — not re-parsed from prose.
4. **End-to-end in a browser**, not curl: a rate-limited checkout still shows the quantified wait. This is the criterion that catches the frontend coupling above, and it is the only one that would have caught #409.

Refs #409, #410, #412
title: Rate-limit 429 body is hand-rolled JSON, not RFC 7807 — contradicts the agent-readiness contract

body:
Found while fixing #409 (PR #410). Split out because it changes a live API response contract.

## The defect

`RateLimitInterceptor` sets four headers on every throttled response — `Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset` (`core-java/.../security/RateLimitInterceptor.java:48-51`).

**None of them is readable by a browser.** Only the CORS-safelisted response headers are exposed to JS cross-origin; everything else needs `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. `CorsConfig.java` sets `setAllowedOrigins` (line 25) and never calls `setExposedHeaders` — `grep -rn 'exposedHeaders|Access-Control-Expose' core-java/src/main/java core-java/src/main/resources` returns **nothing**.

The storefront calls the API cross-origin (`localhost:3000` → `localhost:9090`), so every one of those headers is stripped before the client sees it.

## Two client paths already depend on them, and both silently degrade

1. **`frontend/lib/public-fetch-retry.ts:52-67`** — `getRetryDelayMs()` reads `response.headers["retry-after"]` and, per its own docstring, *"Honours the server Retry-After header … Otherwise falls back to capped exponential backoff."* The header is never present, so it **always** takes the fallback. The server's actual wait is ignored on every retry. Nothing reports this: a silent fallback looks identical to a working one.
2. **`frontend/lib/order-error.ts`** (added by #410) hit the same wall. Measured in a real browser 2026-08-01: `curl -I` showed `Retry-After: 19`, the unit tests asserted the quantified copy, and the page rendered *"please wait a moment"* every time. It now parses the number out of the response **body** as a workaround — which works, but only because the body happens to restate it in prose.

This is the "structural green over a dead feature" shape: `curl` proves the header is sent, and that says nothing about whether any browser can read it.

## Proposed fix

Add to `CorsConfig`:

```java
config.setExposedHeaders(List.of(
    "Retry-After", "X-RateLimit-Limit", "X-RateLimit-Remaining", "X-RateLimit-Reset"));
```

Configurable rather than hardcoded, consistent with `cors.allowed-origins`.

## Acceptance criteria — each must be shown to FAIL first

1. **In a real browser**, not curl: a throttled `fetch` to the public API resolves `response.headers.get('Retry-After')` to the number. **Fail direction:** revert `setExposedHeaders` and confirm it reads `null` — that is the current state, so capture it as the "before" measurement first.
2. `getRetryDelayMs()` returns the header-derived delay rather than its backoff. **Fail direction:** with the header hidden, prove it returns exactly `BASE_DELAY_MS * 2**attempt` — i.e. show the current behaviour is the fallback, not a coincidence.
3. `order-error.ts` still quantifies the wait with the **body parser disabled**, proving the header path now actually executes.
4. A CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) response carries `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` with all four names.

## Note

Once this lands, `order-error.ts`'s body-parsing fallback becomes redundant but should be **kept** — it is the only thing that works if this config is ever lost, and its tests already cover both paths independently.

Refs #409, #410
title: CORS: Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* are never visible to the browser — two client retry paths silently degrade

body:
Found while verifying #408 on the merged runtime (`main` @ `0bc52826`, compose stack `:3000`, frontend rebuilt from that commit and `check-runtime-freshness` 4/4 FRESH).

## What happens

`POST /public/shops/{slug}/orders` returns **201 with a real order**, and the checkout page never advances to the confirmation state.

```
[POST 201] http://localhost:9090/public/shops/mama-ades-kitchen/orders
  {"orderNumber":"ORD-00000000-20260801-C2B5967F","status":"PENDING",
   "subtotalPennies":1349,"deliveryFeePennies":350,"totalAmountPennies":1699,
   "clientSecret":null,...}

[url]   http://localhost:3000/shop/mama-ades-kitchen/checkout   <- never leaves checkout
[toast] [""]                                                    <- empty
```

At failure the page snapshot still shows the **fully populated checkout form** — `heading "Checkout"`, `paragraph: 2 items · £13.49`, `button "Place order · £16.99"` (enabled), address filled.

## Why this matters

The order exists. The customer is shown no confirmation and a still-populated basket, so the obvious next action is to press **Place order** again — **duplicate orders**. The COD path takes no payment online, so nothing else stops it.

## What is established

- The order **is** created server-side: 201, real order number, correct totals.
- The success branch in `frontend/app/shop/[slug]/checkout/page.tsx` did **not** run: it calls `clearCart()` then `setCodConfirmation(...)`, and the cart was still populated at failure.
- It is **not** the empty-cart early return at `page.tsx:260` — that branch would have replaced the form, and the form was still rendered.
- It is **not** a configured client timeout: no `timeout:` is set on the API client, and the endpoint responds in milliseconds (3 samples, 0.004–0.015 s on the reject path).

## What is NOT established

**The mechanism.** Deliberately not guessed. It is intermittent and appears **load-sensitive**, matching the pattern #404 and #406 both record for this suite:

| run | machine | result |
|---|---|---|
| full suite, quiet | `:3000` | Mailhog test **passed** |
| full suite, loaded | `:3000` | **failed** |
| isolated re-run ×2 | `:3000` | **failed** (18.9 s, 19.2 s) |
| direct probe | `:3000` | **failed** — 201 captured, no confirmation |

## Reproduce

```bash
cd frontend
PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
  npx playwright test e2e/storefront-flows.spec.ts -g "order confirmation email"
```

Fails on `expect(getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order confirmed!' })).toBeVisible()` at `e2e/storefront-flows.spec.ts:113` (inside the `placeOrder` helper).

## Note on discovery

This was only observable after #408 fixed the CSP block that made customer sign-in fail entirely — so this path had an unreliable-at-best confirmation and nothing watched it. Same theme as #404: CI runs `e2e/public-layout.spec.ts` only, 2 of 128 tests.

Refs #404, #408
